title: Shell stitch — five trebles, one base
subtitle: A fan of stitches into a single point — the blanket and border classic
excerpt: Shell stitch is five (or any odd number of) trebles worked into the same base stitch or chain space, fanning out like a shell. The foundation of shell-stitch blankets, shawl edgings, and lace borders across Victorian and modern crochet.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — the shell stitch in border and edging patterns. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 2 (1887) — shell stitch blanket borders.

glossaryTerms.definition: Five (or more) trebles worked into the same stitch or chain space, fanning out to form a shell or scallop shape. The base is one point; the top spreads wide.

heroPrompt: A swatch of shell stitch in soft blue DK cotton, three rows of shells alternating with chain spaces, showing the scalloped surface, close-up on natural linen in soft daylight.

content.text: puts five trebles into the same base — a chain space, the centre of a previous shell, or a stitch. They fan out from the single entry point into the classic scallop shape. The alternating pattern of shells and chain spaces creates the shell-stitch fabric used on baby blankets, dishcloths, and shawl edges across the published pattern record.
Chain a multiple of 6 plus 3 for the foundation. This example uses ch 27 for 4 shells.
Row 1 (foundation row): dc in 2nd ch from hook, *sk 2 ch, 5 tr in next ch (one shell made), sk 2 ch, dc in next ch; repeat from * across. Turn.

Row 2: ch 3 (counts as tr), 2 tr in the first dc (half shell at edge), *dc in the 3rd tr of the next shell (the centre), 5 tr in the next dc; repeat from * to last shell, dc in centre of last shell, 3 tr in the last dc. Turn.
Row 3: ch 1, dc in first tr, *5 tr in the next dc (centre stitch), dc in centre of next shell; repeat from * ending with dc in top of ch-3. Turn.

attrs.title: Shell sizes
attrs.body: The standard shell is 5 trebles. A 3tr shell is more closed and dense; a 7tr shell is a deeper fan shape. For most blanket patterns, 5tr is the right size for DK cotton at 4 mm. Bulky yarn at 6 mm usually uses a 3tr shell. Fine cotton at 2.5 mm suits a 7tr shell.

items.symptom: Shells don't line up row to row
items.cause: Missing the centre stitch of the previous shell (the 3rd treble) on the return row
items.fix: Count the trebles of each shell and mark the 3rd one. The dc on the return row always goes into the 3rd treble — the centre of the shell.

items.cause: Full shells at the edges where a half shell should be
items.fix: The edge treatment is a half shell (2 tr or 3 tr) to keep the edge straight. Check the pattern's edge instruction before starting each row.

content.text: Fan stitch is a wider version — seven or more trebles from a single point. V-stitch is a two-treble shell with a chain space between, giving an open lacy look. The granny square uses cluster pairs with chain corners that derive from the same shell principle.
